Ecological Identity What Shaped Me

Nov 16, 2010 • Janice Cotcher

Looking back on my life, it is hard to list all of my experiences that have shaped my ecological identity. Here are just a few that come to mind:

As we’d walk through the park near our house, mom would pick up any garbage we’d come across, put it in her pocket then throw it away when we came to a garbage can. It wasn’t anything that I was taught explicitly but something we just did.

In grade 6, my teacher asked the class “Who has ever littered?” Everyone put up their hand except for me. My teacher didn’t believe me that I had never thrown any trash on the ground. I told him “I tried to throw a gum wrapper on the ground once but I felt so bad I turned around and picked it up.” This certainly did not endear me to my classmates.

# I know this really dates me but I remember watching an Earth Day TV special when I was 11 years old (April 22, 1990). Even though it was the 20th anniversary of Earth Day, it was the first time I was ever aware of its existence. The Exxon Valdez oil spill and the hole in the ozone over Antarctica and the deforestation of the Amazon Rainforest were all hot topics of the moment so it certainly felt like the time to save the environment. At the time, the only actions I knew about taking were being “ozone friendly” and recyclable products.

# When I was in grade 8, Environment Canada produced a handbook on conservation in the home. I don’t even remember how I received it but read the entire thing from cover to cover. I was so excited by everything I learned, I wrote a speech on conservation for a Grade 8 class oratory competition. My teacher loved my speech but, once again, it did not endear me to my classmates.

# My maternal Grandparents didn’t have running water or electricity in their part of Saskatchewan until the mid-1950s. Still to this day, water from comes a well so conservation is an everyday necessity. My grandpa told me that he doesn’t consider himself an environmentalist but it is just common sense that you “never use more than your share”. Living on limited resources is a realty they are faced with everyday. I think this is a concept that too many others are too far removed from.

# When I returned to university to complete my BSc, I was struck by the conservation efforts made by the Physics students:

  • Paper is always reused before it is recycled. Most don’t buy their own paper for assignments but re-use paper from the recycle bins in the library.
  • Not waiting to throw away plant matter, there is a vermi-compost in the student workroom.

It was refreshing to meet a group of people who were always striving to use less resources and discover new ways to help their environment.
